prize_parts.citation: for the experimental realisation of Hubbard models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition to fermionic and single-site-resolved quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter

statement.case_for: I keep B020 first, but I change the trio. The scientific core is unchanged: a textbook many-body model, the Bose-Hubbard model, became a laboratory system whose parameters are known and tunable, and the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition (2002) showed it. Fermionic Hubbard physics with Fermi gases in lattices and quantum-gas microscopes then let one see correlations site by site. This is a result about how interacting quantum systems behave, which is the kind of question about nature I care about, and the comparison with quantum Monte Carlo and strong-coupling theory is quantitative, reproduced in many laboratories over two decades. Round 1 changed my mind on credit. I had kept Zoller to represent the proposal. But the 1998 optical-lattice proposal had five authors, and Cirac is one of them, so crediting Zoller alone as 'the proposal' singles out one author of a joint paper and sits badly with his and Cirac's presence in B006. Esslinger was an author of the 2002 Mott paper and led the fermionic Hubbard work. The three experimentalists therefore match the observations that the citation names, and the proposal can be acknowledged in the citation text and in the committee's motivation without a name. In answer to Olsson's request for a single original experiment, I name it: the 2002 Mott-insulator transition, and the citation is anchored on it and on its two direct extensions, fermions and single-site imaging.
statement.case_against: This is still a programme and not a single event. The doped Hubbard model and the pseudogap, the payoff that would settle the case, have not been reached, and the committee may reasonably say a prize should wait for that. Dropping Zoller leaves the theory proposal uncredited by name, and Jaksch, Cirac and Hansch also remain outside the trio, so the credit will look incomplete whichever three are chosen. BEC (2001), the 1997 cooling prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems are close in history, and the citation must say that this is many-body physics of interacting lattice systems and not condensation or cooling. If the committee wants a sharply bounded result with clean two-name attribution, B024 is the stronger fit.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the discovery-versus-technology worry bites B020 harder than B024, since the clocks give a single repeatedly confirmed number while simulation is still working toward the doped Hubbard model, and that Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger fits what experiments established better than my Zoller trio.
responses.response: On the trio he has persuaded me, and I now propose Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger. My reason is a specific one: the 1998 proposal was a five-author paper including Cirac, so one theory name picks an arbitrary slice of it, while the Mott observation and the fermionic and microscope work are what the experiments established. On the larger question I still disagree. A single number at 10^-18 is a superb result, but the clock tests known physics more sharply, whereas the Mott transition and single-site correlation measurements showed how interacting atoms in a lattice organise themselves. That said, his case is strong on reproducibility and attribution, and B024 is my first alternative. If the committee insists on a bounded and finished result, I would move to it.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B020 with Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, said fermionic Hubbard physics would have no experimental voice under my trio, and said she could support a Zoller trio only if the discovery is the proposal plus the Mott observation.
responses.response: She is right that the fermionic part, which speaks most directly to correlated-electron theory, was unrepresented in my trio, and that was a real flaw. I have changed to her trio, so we now agree on the names. I would still say, against her own caution, that the doped Hubbard model is not required for the discovery: the Mott transition and single-site observation already told us something new. I take her point that a platform is not a result, and I think the citation has to name the transition and the fermionic and microscope results explicitly and not just 'quantum simulation'.

responses.point: Olsson asked whether I see one original experiment the citation can name rather than a field of simulation, and said that would raise B020 for her; she also stressed that five credited names make any trio omit someone with a real claim.
responses.response: Yes, I do: the 2002 observation of the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition in an optical lattice, which is a clean experiment with a clean theoretical comparison. The citation should be anchored on that, with the fermionic Hubbard studies and the microscopes as its established extensions. I accept her point that some name is always omitted, and I do not think the committee can avoid that here, as with B021 or B025. Her own candidate, B005, I respect as finished and verified, but the attribution questions she raises for MgO, Parkin against Yuasa and the omitted theorists, are as hard as mine, and that is what keeps me from supporting it.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B021 first, regards B020 as diffuse with overlaps to the 2001, 2012 and 2022 prizes, and says the pairing mechanism should not delay a prize, as with the 1987 prize on high-temperature superconductivity.
responses.response: His comparison with 1987 is fair, and I withdraw part of my objection: a prize does not need the mechanism. My remaining concern with B021 is different. It is about eight years old, the sample dependence from twist-angle disorder is large, and the parallel experimental groups and Cao cannot be named. I would not block it, but I would prefer to see it later. On B020 being diffuse, the narrowed citation and the change of trio are my answer, and I would add that prior prizes honoured condensation and single-system control, while interacting lattice many-body physics is a separate step.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the proposal to be credited by name, in which case Zoller would have to replace one of the experimentalists, and how Cirac's equal role in the 1998 paper and Zoller's presence in B006 should be handled.
Whether quantum simulation counts as a discovery about nature or a technique, and whether the doped Hubbard question should postpone the prize.
Whether B024 should be preferred if the committee wants a sharply bounded result, and whether lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
I rely on memory for the author lists and priority details of the 1998 proposal and the 2002 Mott paper, and Hansch and Jaksch are outside the credited list.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a long collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I have worked with Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato. None of these people is credited in any shortlisted entry. I know of no direct personal or institutional connection to Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller, Cirac, Blatt, Katori or Ye. Atomic physics is close to B020, B024 and B006, which may colour my judgement without being a formal conflict, and I have no change to report since round 1.
